title: Who Verifies the Verifier? Co-EvolvingInspectable Graders with Self-Improving Agents

paper.title: Who Verifies the Verifier? Co-Evolving Inspectable Graders with Self-Improving Agents
paper.abstract: Abstract We changed the agent: did it actually get better? Every self-improving agent loop answers this hundreds of times, and every answer comes from a verifier. On open-ended tasks none exists, so the loop is handed a hand-written rubric or a bare LLM judge grading output from a model like itself, inviting reward hacking and shared blind spots. We make the verifier the evolving object: an inspectable expression over small, mostly deterministic drawback detectors, synthesized from clustered failures, gated at birth, and selected for agreement with a ten-item anchored reference set plus consensus over unlabeled outputs, never for the agent’s score. On MBPP+ it gains + 0.21 +0.21 held-out agreement over the hand-authored seed composition, on every seed, and ends ahead of the bare LLM judge it contains. One finding should change how co-evolved verifiers are validated: removing the anchor guards collapses the verifier into a vacuous always-pass grader, yet that collapsed verifier trains skills just as well . Downstream task score cannot certify a self-evolved verifier. Score does answer sufficiency, and there an evolved verifier can substitute: Double Ratchet , pairing the verifier with a lifecycle-managed skill loop, retains 88–110% of the lift that ground truth or a rubric buys the same loop, across code generation, enterprise text-to-SQL, and reference-free report generation. When evolved skills gamed the report rubric, an outer judge caught it and one added detector repaired it; the judge itself was wrong until given the task contract.

When evolved skills gamed the report rubric, an outer judge caught it and one added detector repaired it; the judge itself was wrong until given the task contract. 1 Introduction We update an agent’s prompt, add a tool, or change its reasoning strategy: did it actually get better? A self-improving agent asks this every round. The standard recipe wraps a frozen language model in a loop that writes skills, retrieves them, measures their contribution, and retires the ones that hurt [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] , and it consumes one expensive ingredient per round: a verifier that says whether an attempt passed. On code benchmarks that ingredient is free, since unit tests exist. In deployed systems it is the bottleneck, and the industry’s own products document the workaround: Claude’s managed agents have developers hand-write outcome rubrics for a separate grader [ 4 ] , and Codex’s Record & Replay has a human demonstrate each workflow once [ 5 ] . Both are manual substitutes for a missing verifier, supplied one rubric or demonstration at a time. This paper automates that step: can an agent’s verifier be evolved from a handful of anchored examples, drive learning as well as ground truth, and not be gamed in the process? Two clarifications determine how every result below should be read. First, the verifier, or grader, is the function that grades one output , and it is the only thing that evolves; the task sets and their references are fixed before any loop starts, so no result here can come from an easier test. Second, in our target setting no accurate verifier exists , so there is no baseline verifier to beat: the yardstick is how much of the improvement an accurate verifier would have enabled a system recovers without one. Matching a ground-truth-driven reference loop is the win condition, not a consolation. The design rests on one stance about verification. We rarely know what good is, but given an output we can usually find drawbacks , so a clean verdict means no known drawback was found rather than certified correctness. That framing is what makes bootstrapping possible, and it determines the shape of the artifact (Figure 1 ): the verifier is an expression over a pool of small typed detectors, each checking one failure class, synthesized from clustered failures, gated at birth, scored by marginal contribution, and retired when useless. Detectors span the three cost tiers a real deployment already has (static checks, execution against a sandbox or a live warehouse, and narrow judge queries), so composing them folds heterogeneous signals into one grader instead of trusting a single scalar. Being mostly deterministic, they fail differently from the model being graded, which is what resists the shared-blind-spot collusion a bare LLM judge invites; being a readable expression, the grader localizes a failure to a nameable check that can be repaired by hand (§ 5.4 ). A verifier that grades the loop that produced it is an obvious Goodhart hazard [ 6 , 7 ] , so anchor discipline is strict and load-bearing. Selection never asks whether the agent scores well: it asks whether the verifier agrees with a tiny anchored reference set, the only supervised signal verifier evolution reads, and with detector consensus on a large unlabeled set. A separate locked set is read by no verifier loop and serves only for verifier evaluation and skill-side rollback. We test by ablation whether that discipline carries the safety load, and the answer bears directly on how this community should validate co-evolved verifiers at all. Our contributions are as follows. • Verifier evolution, with an objective that needs no downstream metric. We formulate the grading function, rather than the artifact being graded, as the evolving object: anchored search over compositions of atomic drawback detectors under a lifecycle of synthesis, birth gating, marginal-contribution scoring, and retirement. Selection is recall-weighted agreement with a ten-item anchor times reliability-weighted consensus over unlabeled outputs, and the result beats both the hand-authored composition it starts from and the bare LLM judge it contains. • Where the safety lives, and why task score cannot find it. Anchor discipline, not the detector lifecycle, is load-bearing for verifiers, inverting the lesson from skill evolution. Since a collapsed verifier trains skills as well as a valid one, validating a self-evolved verifier by downstream performance is unsound : the most natural validation experiment would certify a grader that passes everything. • Double Ratchet, and a reward-hacking episode end to end. Co-evolving the verifier with a skill loop retains 88–110% of the lift ground truth buys, across three task areas. On the reference-free task we document proxy gaming caught by an outer judge, repaired by one added detector, and an audit of the auditor showing the outer judge needs the task contract. Figure 1: What evolves. Center : the verifier selected on MBPP+, verbatim, as an expression over typed detectors spanning the three cost tiers, with each leaf’s verdict on one held-out attempt. Naming the failure class rather than emitting a scalar is what turns a graded attempt into a usable failure capsule. Left : the premise, no oracle verifier and ten anchored examples. Right : the consumer, a lifecycle-managed skill loop [ 1 ] adopted unchanged, whose training the evolved verifier grades. Bottom : the anchor guards. 2 Related work Self-evolving agents assume the verifier. Agents grow skill libraries, revise from failure traces, and bank reusable experience as insights, manuals, memories, or workflows [ 2 , 3 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 ] ; a recent wave evolves, analyzes, and benchmarks such libraries [ 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 ] , and two surveys map the landscape [ 20 , 21 ] . Ratchet [ 1 , 22 ] showed that unmanaged LLM-authored libraries drift and that a minimal lifecycle restores the gains; that published loop is adopted unchanged here as the skill-side component and is not a contribution of this work. Other lines search over agent code [ 23 ] , inherit the architecture-search tradition [ 24 ] , or optimize prompts and pipelines against a metric [ 25 , 26 , 27 , 28 ] . All of them optimize against a verification signal taken as given. We evolve that signal, and ask which part of the discipline carries the safety load once the grader itself moves. Searched objectives are scored by a metric that already exists. Existing work evolves loss functions [ 29 ] , whole learning algorithms [ 30 ] , symbolic pruning metrics [ 31 ] , and program code [ 32 ] against supplied evaluators. The search space is analogous, primitive checks composed into a program, but the fitness differs in kind: each is scored by a metric taken as valid, with AlphaEvolve stating outright that progress must be machine-gradable, the precondition our regime lacks. We supply the missing foothold: anchored agreement plus consensus regularization in place of a downstream score. Learned graders trade the assumption for opacity. Reward design is delicate even in classical RL [ 33 ] ; RLHF reward models are over-optimized by the policies they train and misspecification produces systematic gaming [ 34 , 7 , 35 , 36 , 37 ] ; AI-feedback and self-rewarding setups let the model judge itself [ 38 , 39 ] ; and LLM judges are widely audited for bias [ 40 , 41 , 42 , 43 ] . We share the reward-hacking hazard but not the structure: our grader is a composition of typed detectors optimized to predict an anchor it never trains on, so it can be read and repaired by hand, and its agent-facing use is confined to training. Agent-as-judge co-evolution [ 44 ] is closest in spirit and validates the judge through the system it grades, which § 5.2 shows a vacuous grader also passes. The evaluators nearest our tasks fix in advance what we synthesize, gate, and retire: CodeScore [ 45 ] predicts functional correctness from the execution-labeled supervision we take to be missing, and SQLHD [ 46 ] needs no ground truth but fixes a hand-authored family of metamorphic relations [ 47 ] . Either could be one typed detector in our pool, so we read them as components rather than competitors, while agentic text-to-SQL pipelines [ 48 ] improve the solver, an orthogonal axis. We use MBPP+ [ 49 , 50 ] and Spider 2.0 [ 51 ] as hard anchors for certifying evolved verifiers, in the execution-graded tradition of HumanEval [ 52 ] , not as leaderboard entries. 3 The verifier and its evolution Let a task family come with tasks t t and a frozen solver mapping t t to an output y y . A verifier M M maps ( t , y ) (t,y) to a verdict in { pass , fail , abstain } \{\textsc{pass},\textsc{fail},\textsc{abstain}\} , and M M is what we search over, with tasks and references held fixed. Three disjoint splits play the usual roles with one twist each. train is large and unlabeled: solver outputs here expose where candidate verifiers disagree or abstain, and in co-evolution the evolved verifier grades these tasks for the skill loop. dev is tiny and anchored, ten items throughout: each task carries a golden reference against which a teacher emits soft pass/fail labels, the only supervised signal verifier evolution reads. Those references grade only the ten tasks that carry them, while the evolved verifier must grade arbitrary outputs on tasks that have none. Dev is deliberately small because sparse anchoring is the realistic regime: fresh labels in deployed systems arrive as a trickle of demonstrations and incident reviews. test is locked against the verifier: it holds the strongest available reference (unit tests, official execution comparison, the report rubric) and no part of verifie
